Daniel’s analogy is suggestive, but it quietly swaps the meaning of “atomic” from a *specification* (“this operation appears to take effect at a single instant”) to a *physical event* that must achieve a perfect bifurcation in continuous time. In concurrency theory, atomicity is not “the world truly has a sharp knife-edge instant”; it is an interface contract that defines a total order consistent with real-time precedence—what [linearizability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearizability) formalizes (Herlihy & Wing). The whole point is that a messy, continuous implementation can still be *observationally discrete* if it guarantees that every execution has a well-defined “as-if” order. Daniel’s framing makes it sound like the abstraction requires literal physical discontinuity; it doesn’t.

Where the “dice on its corner forever” story *does* map well is at the hardware boundary: there are known places where continuous physics leaks into discrete computation. Clock-domain crossings and arbiters can enter **metastability**, hovering near a threshold in a way that is not safely capturable as a clean 0/1 within bounded time; engineers can only reduce its probability and contain its effects, not banish it by decree ([Metastability (electronics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metastability_(electronics))). That is the closest real analogue to Daniel’s “adversarial initial condition”: not that an adversary can always force failure, but that the “unstable equilibrium” is structurally present in the physics, so designs rely on synchronizers, timing margins, and probabilistic guarantees rather than absolute elimination.

So does this mean race conditions are impossible to prevent? At the *program* level, no: you can prevent data races by construction (message passing, immutability, ownership types, or properly specified locks/atomics) because the property is defined relative to a model of allowed interleavings. At the *physical* level, Daniel’s worry becomes sharper: the discrete model itself rests on assumptions about time, ordering, and eventual signal resolution—assumptions that are engineered, tested, and overwhelmingly reliable, but not metaphysically absolute. The more precise reframing is: you can eliminate races **within a chosen abstraction**, while accepting that the abstraction is ultimately implemented on a substrate where “perfect bifurcation” is approximated, not fundamental—a point already implicit in Lamport’s insistence that ordering is a model we impose to reason about systems ([Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/time-clocks.pdf)).
